quote: Man kann zunächst bei der Differentialgl. $y'' = \lambda A(x) y$ fragen, ob $A(x)$ durch die Angabe der [-xxx-] singulären Werte $\lambda_1, \lambda_2, \ldots$ [-x-] völlig bestimmt ist und die [-xxx-] [-xxx-] Werte $\lambda_1, \lambda_2, \ldots$ beliebig variirt werden dürfen.
english: One can first ask, for the differential equation y'' = λA(x)y, whether A(x) is completely determined by specifying the singular values λ1, λ2, ..., and whether the values λ1, λ2, ... may be varied arbitrarily.
topic: Hilbert discusses the dependence of solutions of differential equations on a parameter λ, noting that they have poles at the special values of λ, and asks general questions about singularities and branching in the parameter and about whether the coefficient A(x) is determined by the singular values.

triage.modern_statement: This is the inverse spectral problem for the vibrating string. Take the boundary-value problem y'' = λA(x)y on an interval with fixed boundary conditions, for example a string with density A(x) ≥ 0 and fixed ends. It has a discrete set of eigenvalues λ1, λ2, .... The first question is uniqueness: does that sequence of eigenvalues determine the coefficient (density) A(x) completely? The second question is characterization: can any sequence (subject to suitable growth conditions) arise as such a spectrum, so that the λ_n can be varied freely? Today this falls under inverse Sturm–Liouville theory, and in particular M. G. Krein's spectral theory of strings.
triage.answered_by: Ambarzumian (1929) gave the first inverse eigenvalue result. Borg (1946) showed that one spectrum alone does not in general fix the coefficient, but two spectra (two sets of boundary conditions) do. Gelfand–Levitan (1951) then gave a reconstruction method. For the string form y'' = -λρ(x)y, M. G. Krein (around 1951–1953) determined the density of a string from its frequencies and described which spectral data can occur. I. S. Kats and others continued this work. The answer to both of Hilbert's questions is therefore: not from one spectrum alone, but yes from extra spectral data, and admissible spectra can be characterized.

evidence.claim: Borg proved that the inverse problem of recovering a Sturm–Liouville potential from two spectra has a unique solution and is locally solvable; Gelfand and Levitan developed a method to reconstruct the potential from spectral data.
Ambarzumian's 1929 result was the first inverse Sturm–Liouville theorem, recovering the zero potential from one spectrum in a special case. Borg's 1946 theorem is the founding result of the field.

M. G. Krein wrote 'Determination of the density of an inhomogeneous symmetric string from the spectrum of its frequencies' (Dokl.), which is exactly the problem of recovering A(x) in y'' = λA(x)y from its eigenvalues. I. S. Kats studied uniqueness cases for the inverse string problem.
Krein's spectral theory of strings and its inverse problem remained under study afterwards, e.g. Kotani (1973) and Kac–Krein.
Inverse spectral problems for Krein strings are still being researched, e.g. star graphs of Krein strings (Eckhardt).

triage.why: Hilbert asks whether the coefficient of y'' = λA(x)y is fixed by its eigenvalues and whether those eigenvalues can be prescribed freely. That is the classical inverse Sturm–Liouville / inverse string problem. Ambarzumian, Borg, Gelfand–Levitan and Krein settled it: one spectrum is generally not enough (only special or symmetric cases), extra data such as a second spectrum or norming constants does determine A, and Krein's theory characterizes which spectral data are admissible. The question is not among Hilbert's 23 published problems. I found no source that explicitly links Hilbert's note to these results, so the identification rests on the mathematical match alone. The exact boundary conditions Hilbert had in mind are also unclear from the fragment, which is why confidence is medium. The field (inverse spectral theory) is still active.
